subject: chemistry
title: Atomic Structure Adventure 2: Electron configuration and orbitals
welcome_lead: Today you'll fill s, p, d orbitals — and write electron configurations.
meta_desc: Chemistry — electron configuration, sub-shells s/p/d, Aufbau, Hund's rule, ionisation energies.
final_note: You learned electrons fill shells via Aufbau (1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p), each sub-shell holds 2/6/10, and IE evidence supports this.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Each shell n splits into sub-shells s, p, d, f:

- n=1: 1s (2 e⁻)
- n=2: 2s + 2p (2 + 6 = 8 e⁻)
- n=3: 3s + 3p + 3d (2 + 6 + 10 = 18 e⁻)
- n=4: 4s + 4p + 4d + 4f (32 e⁻)

Each orbital holds max 2 electrons with opposite spin (Pauli).

Aufbau filling order (energy-based):

1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p 5s 4d 5p 6s 4f 5d 6p.

Examples:
- Na (Z=11): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹
- Ca (Z=20): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s²
- Fe (Z=26): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶ 4s² (often written this way)

Exceptions: Cr [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ and Cu [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ — stable half/full d.

First IE: M(g) → M⁺(g) + e⁻.

Across period: IE generally rises (more protons, same shell).

Down group: IE falls (more shells, shielding).

Successive IE plots show jumps when moving to inner shells — directly evidencing shell structure.

Nature of science: IE data confirmed quantum mechanical orbital model.

Why are most transition metal complex ions coloured?
options: Transition metal ions are coloured because they have a half-full d-subshell which naturally absorbs light.
Ligands split the d-orbitals into two energy levels; electrons absorb visible light to jump between them (d-d transitions), and the complementary colour is transmitted.
Transition metals are coloured because their nuclei emit photons in the visible range.
Transition metals have variable oxidation states because they can gain protons easily.

mcqs.q: Why can transition metals show variable oxidation states?
options: Transition metals have variable oxidation states because they have many shells of electrons.
The 4s and 3d orbitals are similar in energy, so different numbers of electrons can be removed without a large energy cost.
The forward reaction stops once the reverse reaction begins.
